text: Everything in this chapter so far produces the same kind of output: a finding. The last lesson in this chapter is about what has to happen next, because a finding that gets written up and then filed away was never actually worth finding in the first place.

Picture a real one: killing one of three payment-service pods dropped checkout success to 94 percent, because all three pods turned out to share one underlying database connection pool nobody had mapped. Writing that down in a wiki page and moving on leaves the system exactly as vulnerable as before — except now there's documented proof the team knew about a weakness and chose not to fix it, which is a worse position to be in once it causes a real outage.

A genuine single point of failure like that demands an actual architecture change, not a caveat in a runbook. Name the SPOF precisely. File it as owned work — a ticket, a named owner, a target date, exactly like a bug or a postmortem action item. Build the real redundancy: separate connection pools, a cache replica, spreading a dependency across availability zones, a fallback path to a second processor. And then re-run the exact same chaos experiment to confirm the steady-state hypothesis actually holds now.

That last step matters more than it sounds like it should. A fix isn't done when the code merges — it's done when the original experiment is run again and checkout success rate stays at 99.9 percent instead of dropping to 94. Treating findings this way also closes the loop back to earlier in this path: review them in the same forum that already tracks error budget burn and postmortem action items, so a known SPOF competes for priority against feature work visibly, on the record, instead of losing by default because no one owns it.

That's the whole arc of this chapter: a precise hypothesis, a safely injected failure, a full game day testing people as well as systems, and a finding that only counts once it's verified fixed. Chapter 4 picks up from here and goes deeper into disaster recovery architecture itself — DR patterns at real enterprise complexity, dependency mapping, and automating failover instead of relying on a runbook at 3 a.m.
